top_articles.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
top_articles.title_original: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
top_articles.summary: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. Codex voice mode I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. Talking to my computer I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results. Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist . We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code. What we built We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice: A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for that Four working imports: The most recent Substack items via RSS Every other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried /api/v1/archive directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen Spinner All of my published monthly newsletters from my simonw/monthly-newsletter-archive GitHub repository My most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repository The /newsletters/ and /newsletters/2026/ public archive pages Newsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepage Weekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pages Integration with my site search engine It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while. Finishing it with a review Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request. I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead. You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR . I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR. The end result You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page , or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter . The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages. GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen. Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driver OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though. I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code. This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent. I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words. I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace! The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead. top_articles.summary: Release: llm-gemini 0.35 I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan. Here are the low, medium and high pelicans . As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5. Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness. One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models. When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. (I used ChatGPT to edit that chart ! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.) Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars , here's a Fabergé egg it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles . top_articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.title_original: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. top_articles.title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.title_original: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.10942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

top_articles.title: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
top_articles.title_original: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from conversational assistants into Cowork Agents capable of autonomous planning, tool use, and complex task execution. Financial analysis requires these agents to integrate cross-document evidence and perform multistep numerical reasoning, but expert task authoring is costly, while direct LLM synthesis struggles to produce challenging tasks with reliable answers. We introduce Navalia, a framework for Cowork Agents that combines verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. Using corporate financial reports as its data source, Navalia semantically selects supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructs executable computation chains to generate analytical tasks with traceable evidence and actual data dependencies between steps. We further use independent LLM review and programmatic checks to verify evidence consistency and answer correctness. The verified tasks are then used for trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve long-horizon task execution. Navalia, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, achieves consistent gains over the base model across all five benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, and Workspace-Bench-Lite. These results demonstrate that Navalia improves evidence integration, tool use, and long-horizon task execution capabilities and generalizes to broader Cowork settings, including general office tasks.

top_articles.title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
top_articles.title_original: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.

top_articles.title: 开发者将破解后的索尼 PS5 当作本地 AI 服务器：利用 GPU 加速运行 27B 参数 Qwen3.8-27B 模型，速度达 20.9 token/s
top_articles.title_original: 开发者将破解后的索尼 PS5 当作本地 AI 服务器：利用 GPU 加速运行 27B 参数 Qwen3.8-27B 模型，速度达 20.9 token/s
top_articles.summary: IT之家 10 月 17 日消息，据外媒 Wccftech 报道，开发者 abhi245y 基于资深 AI 工程师 Mert Cobanov 的 PS5LM（ llama.cpp 移植项目），开发了原生 GPU 应用 PS5LM Plus，让经过破解的 PS5 主机能够在本地运行 Qwen3.8-27B 等大型语言模型。 IT之家获悉，PS5LM 的早期版本主要依靠 CPU 运行模型，执行 27B 参数模型时，平均每分钟只能生成约 1 个 token。为提升性能，开发者 abhi245y  移植了 Mesa 开源项目中的 AMD RADV 驱动，并通过 Vulkan 计算接口让 llama.cpp 能够作为原生应用在 PS5 上运行。这项改动将可用内存从约 6GB 提升至 11.4GB，使主机能够运行经过高度量化的 Qwen3.8-27B 模型。 得益于 PS5 较高的内存带宽（448GB/s），Qwen3.8-27B 的生成速度可达每秒 20.9 个 token。测试期间，GPU 使用率达到 100%，CPU 使用率仅为 2%。对于规模更小的模型，PS5 还能实现更高的生成速度，例如 Gemma 4 E4B 约为每秒 61 个 token，Llama 3.2 3B 则达到每秒 124 个 token。 除了利用 PS5 的 GPU 加速模型推理，PS5LM Plus 还内置网页聊天界面，并可通过局域网 8081 端口提供 API 服务，用户可通过同一网络中的其他设备访问页面，与本地运行的模型对话。该项目还兼容 OpenAI 和 Anthropic API，方便 opencode、Codex、Claude Code 等工具调用 PS5 上运行的模型。 对于一台主要面向游戏设计的主机而言，PS5 能够充当本地 AI 服务器，为大模型推理提供 GPU 加速，展示了其硬件在游戏之外的应用潜力。不过，该机配备的 16GB RAM 统一内存仍然限制了模型的选择和运行质量。此外，运行原生版 llama.cpp 需要先对 PS5 进行越狱，可能会导致游戏机及 PSN 账号被封禁等风险。

top_articles.summary: IT之家 10 月 15 日消息，英伟达宣布推出开放多模态模型 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL，面向需要持续运行、执行多步骤任务的 AI 智能体。 该模型采用混合专家（MoE）架构，总参数量为 1200 亿，激活参数 120 亿。英伟达称，在单张 GPU 上执行智能体任务时，该模型的吞吐量最高可达到同规模其他开放模型的 5 倍。 据介绍，Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 将推理、指令遵循和工具调用能力，与文本、图像、文档及视频理解能力整合到同一个模型中，可用于代码测试与调试、跨网站信息检索、文档分析、网络安全威胁识别以及视频内容检索等场景。开发者可以利用英伟达 NeMo 工具链，结合自有数据、工具、政策和工作流程进行后训练，并根据业务需求调整模型行为。 英伟达同时公布了多个企业定制案例。例如，AI 数据技术提供商 Scale AI 为媒体娱乐公司 Skydance Corporation 定制了供应商信用处理智能体，相关工作负载的推理成本预计可降低 97.5%、延迟降低 80%。 金融运营平台 Ramp 正将收据图像转换为包含商户、日期和支付信息的结构化 JSON 数据，预计吞吐量最高提升 50%、延迟降低 90%。AI21 与 AI 安全公司 Alice 合作定制模型，用于威胁情报和漏洞分析，相关任务准确率提升 40%。 在模型评测方面，英伟达称 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 在 CharXiv 图表推理基准测试中得分为 80.8%，高于 Nemotron 3 Nano Omni 的 63%；结合 Python 代码解释后，得分达到 84%。 在 Hermes Bench 和 LangChain 行为评估中，该模型分别取得 63.44% 和 87.05%，高于 Nemotron 3 Ultra 的 56.33% 和 84.3%。英伟达还表示，该模型在 OCRBench v2 榜单上属于表现靠前的开放模型之一。 为降低推理开销，Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 采用投机解码、混合精度和上下文复用等技术。英伟达介绍，其 LiLiCorr 投机解码方法在 DGX Spark 上可将词元生成速度最高提升至 2.3 倍。模型还支持 NVFP4 量化，在英伟达 Blackwell 架构上使用 4 位权重和 4 位激活值；在非 Blackwell 平台上，同一检查点使用 4 位权重和 16 位激活值。 英伟达还公布了面向分布式推理的部署优化方案。根据其披露的数据，在使用 16 张 NVIDIA B200 GPU、每名用户每秒生成 50 个词元的测试条件下，NVIDIA Dynamo 配合缓存感知路由、会话亲和性和 KV 缓存卸载，最多可服务 8 倍数量的用户，并将首词元延迟降低 85%。 此次发布还包括基础模型、后训练模型和 NVFP4 量化模型权重，以及训练配方、数据集和强化学习环境。 英伟达表示，Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 在预训练和持续预训练阶段共使用约 26 万亿词元，后训练阶段使用约 380 万个样本，并在数十种环境中进行强化学习。新开放的数据集涵盖智能体工具调用、金融推理、指令遵循、长上下文、公平性和视觉语言理解等领域。 除 Super VL 外，英伟达还推出了两款 Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 端侧模型。Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB 采用 740 亿总参数、90 亿激活参数的 MoE 架构，通过原生 2 位量化将模型压缩至 24GB，面向本地智能体任务，支持 llama.cpp 、vLLM、Ollama、Unsloth 和 LM Studio。Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB 则面向本地语音助手、交互角色和嵌入式界面等场景，计划于 10 月 23 日推出。 IT之家注意到，Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 和 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB 已开放获取，开发者可通过 Hugging Face、OpenRouter、ModelScope 等渠道使用相关模型资源。Super VL 可部署于 DGX Spark、DGX Station、RTX 系统、数据中心或云端；Bolt E4B 4GB 则计划于 10 月 23 日发布。

top_articles.title: Explore Separately, Adopt Selectively: Execution-Guided Tool Use over Large Tool Libraries
top_articles.title_original: Explore Separately, Adopt Selectively: Execution-Guided Tool Use over Large Tool Libraries
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.22688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents must discover relevant tools from large libraries, e.g., thousands of tools, as new needs arise during task execution. When several candidates could satisfy the same need, execution may be required to identify the relevant one. Investigating candidates in a shared trajectory can leave alternatives unexplored or allow failed attempts to influence subsequent reasoning. To address this, we present BRIA (BRanch-Inspect-Adopt), a simple yet effective agent that temporarily isolates candidate investigations in separate branches. Each branch retrieves and executes tools to investigate its candidate; a task agent inspects the resulting execution evidence and adopts only useful results into its continuing trajectory. BRIA retrieves additional tools as new capability needs arise during task execution. We evaluate BRIA on PlanBench-XL and MCP-Atlas using a shared pool of 1897 tools, three language models, and static and adaptive retrieval baselines. Across all settings, BRIA matches or exceeds the strongest retrieval baseline. On MCP-Atlas, it achieves an average claim score of 89.77, compared with 75.40 for MCP-Zero, a gain of 14.37 percentage points. BRIA also lies on the Pareto frontier for task performance and input-token cost.

top_articles.title: RealCLI: Toward a Unified Evaluation of Human-Agent Collaboration for CLI Agents
top_articles.title_original: RealCLI: Toward a Unified Evaluation of Human-Agent Collaboration for CLI Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.22507v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Command-line interface (CLI) agents increasingly execute longer-horizon tasks, yet existing benchmarks either assume that user instructions remain fixed throughout execution or evaluate task outcomes without capturing runtime collaboration quality. In this paper, we present REALCLI, a paired benchmark that unifies the evaluation of task execution and human-agent collaboration quality on realistic CLI tasks. To comprehensively measure collaboration, REALCLI builds a five-dimensional framework, operationalized into 22 sub-dimensions and 51 interaction scenario templates. REALCLI provides two modes for paired comparison: REALCLI-EXEC supplies complete specifications upfront, whereas REALCLI-COLLAB introduces a scripted user that delivers progressive information, corrections, constraint revisions, and authorization decisions. Evaluations reveal profound capability gaps in frontier agents: the best configuration attains an average score of only 49.2%, and when evaluated by the joint collaboration score ($J_{\mathrm{collab}}$), the peak performance reaches merely 37.6%. These results show that task effectiveness diverges sharply from collaboration quality, with models consistently struggling in steerability, trust calibration, and safety boundary management. REALCLI provides a rigorous, reproducible foundation for measuring and advancing collaborative CLI agents.

top_articles.title: AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
top_articles.title_original: AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) possess broad factual knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, but solving complex tasks also requires procedural knowledge about how to act. Existing approaches often represent procedural knowledge through trajectories or bundled skills, limiting flexible reuse across interaction histories. This paper introduces Procedural Atoms, fine-grained and independently applicable units that represent Intent, When, Do, and Avoid guidance. Building on this representation, we propose AtomSD, an Atom-guided Self-Distillation framework in which the learner continually extracts Procedural Atoms from its own successful trajectories and distills them into the evolving policy through Atom-conditioned supervision and task-reward optimization. Comprehensive experiments show that AtomSD consistently outperforms strong reward-based and distillation methods, exceeding the state-of-the-art baseline by up to 9.31 points in average performance. Further analyses demonstrate that the proposed Procedural Atoms provide effective guidance, highlighting the value of atom-level procedural knowledge for policy learning.

top_articles.title: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.title_original: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k, ASE improves average Mean@8 across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks over GRPO by 4.87 and 1.87 percentage points, respectively, under the same rollout budget.

top_articles.title: Expert-Guided Rubrics as Dense Reward Signals for Reinforcement Learning in Non-Verifiable Domains
top_articles.title_original: Expert-Guided Rubrics as Dense Reward Signals for Reinforcement Learning in Non-Verifiable Domains
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they must interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information under domain-specific constraints. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can train such agents from the consequences of their actions, recent successes largely rely on verifiable tasks with automatically computed binary rewards. In non-verifiable retrieval tasks, assessing query quality requires scarce subject-matter expert (SME) judgment that is inherently graded rather than binary. With Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), sparse rewards yield no useful learning signal when all sampled outputs within a group receive the same outcome, causing optimization to stall. We introduce a method that converts a small, fixed investment of SME judgment into a dense reward and combines it with retrieval-based metrics to form a hybrid, GRPO-compatible training signal. Experiments show improvements of up to 6\% in Recall@3 and 6.7\% in MRR@3 compared with sparse-reward baselines.

top_articles.title: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
top_articles.title_original: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic studies of large language models localize function in parameters, attention heads or neurons, but those parts do not specify how one inference unfolds. We treat the ordered layer-state trajectory as the empirical process and test whether layer order defines a measurable computation. Across representative Qwen, Llama and Gemma checkpoints, realized order produced paths 1.60--2.24 times as aligned with their endpoint chord as endpoint-preserving shuffles. The order effect transferred to a lexical task, but was stronger in three random initializations of the same Qwen architecture, identifying an architecture-compatible scaffold rather than a training-specific law. Direct hidden states provided stronger mechanism coordinates than vocabulary readbacks, and a task-defined coordinate made candidate competition computable. After additive interventions failed, local transition actuators selectively controlled internal trajectories across checkpoints. A confidence gate then drove 17 of 87 held-out Qwen closure trajectories across the full-vocabulary top-1 candidate boundary while leaving all 203 non-closure top-1 outputs unchanged. Safety-matched action reassignment performed similarly, locating the gain in selective gating and the bounded actuator family rather than fine-grained dose assignment. Layer order exposes an observable, computable and behaviourally consequential process of transformer inference without establishing a complete theory of LLM dynamics or control of answer correctness.

top_articles.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
top_articles.title_original: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
top_articles.summary: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. Codex voice mode I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. Talking to my computer I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results. Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist . We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code. What we built We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice: A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for that Four working imports: The most recent Substack items via RSS Every other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried /api/v1/archive directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen Spinner All of my published monthly newsletters from my simonw/monthly-newsletter-archive GitHub repository My most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repository The /newsletters/ and /newsletters/2026/ public archive pages Newsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepage Weekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pages Integration with my site search engine It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while. Finishing it with a review Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request. I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead. You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR . I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR. The end result You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page , or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter . The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages. GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen. Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driver OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though. I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code. This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent. I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words. I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace! The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead. top_articles.title_original: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. top_articles.title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.title_original: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.10942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

top_articles.title: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
top_articles.title_original: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from conversational assistants into Cowork Agents capable of autonomous planning, tool use, and complex task execution. Financial analysis requires these agents to integrate cross-document evidence and perform multistep numerical reasoning, but expert task authoring is costly, while direct LLM synthesis struggles to produce challenging tasks with reliable answers. We introduce Navalia, a framework for Cowork Agents that combines verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. Using corporate financial reports as its data source, Navalia semantically selects supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructs executable computation chains to generate analytical tasks with traceable evidence and actual data dependencies between steps. We further use independent LLM review and programmatic checks to verify evidence consistency and answer correctness. The verified tasks are then used for trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve long-horizon task execution. Navalia, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, achieves consistent gains over the base model across all five benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, and Workspace-Bench-Lite. These results demonstrate that Navalia improves evidence integration, tool use, and long-horizon task execution capabilities and generalizes to broader Cowork settings, including general office tasks.

top_articles.title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
top_articles.title_original: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.

top_articles.title: Explore Separately, Adopt Selectively: Execution-Guided Tool Use over Large Tool Libraries
top_articles.title_original: Explore Separately, Adopt Selectively: Execution-Guided Tool Use over Large Tool Libraries
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.22688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents must discover relevant tools from large libraries, e.g., thousands of tools, as new needs arise during task execution. When several candidates could satisfy the same need, execution may be required to identify the relevant one. Investigating candidates in a shared trajectory can leave alternatives unexplored or allow failed attempts to influence subsequent reasoning. To address this, we present BRIA (BRanch-Inspect-Adopt), a simple yet effective agent that temporarily isolates candidate investigations in separate branches. Each branch retrieves and executes tools to investigate its candidate; a task agent inspects the resulting execution evidence and adopts only useful results into its continuing trajectory. BRIA retrieves additional tools as new capability needs arise during task execution. We evaluate BRIA on PlanBench-XL and MCP-Atlas using a shared pool of 1897 tools, three language models, and static and adaptive retrieval baselines. Across all settings, BRIA matches or exceeds the strongest retrieval baseline. On MCP-Atlas, it achieves an average claim score of 89.77, compared with 75.40 for MCP-Zero, a gain of 14.37 percentage points. BRIA also lies on the Pareto frontier for task performance and input-token cost.

top_articles.title: RealCLI: Toward a Unified Evaluation of Human-Agent Collaboration for CLI Agents
top_articles.title_original: RealCLI: Toward a Unified Evaluation of Human-Agent Collaboration for CLI Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.22507v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Command-line interface (CLI) agents increasingly execute longer-horizon tasks, yet existing benchmarks either assume that user instructions remain fixed throughout execution or evaluate task outcomes without capturing runtime collaboration quality. In this paper, we present REALCLI, a paired benchmark that unifies the evaluation of task execution and human-agent collaboration quality on realistic CLI tasks. To comprehensively measure collaboration, REALCLI builds a five-dimensional framework, operationalized into 22 sub-dimensions and 51 interaction scenario templates. REALCLI provides two modes for paired comparison: REALCLI-EXEC supplies complete specifications upfront, whereas REALCLI-COLLAB introduces a scripted user that delivers progressive information, corrections, constraint revisions, and authorization decisions. Evaluations reveal profound capability gaps in frontier agents: the best configuration attains an average score of only 49.2%, and when evaluated by the joint collaboration score ($J_{\mathrm{collab}}$), the peak performance reaches merely 37.6%. These results show that task effectiveness diverges sharply from collaboration quality, with models consistently struggling in steerability, trust calibration, and safety boundary management. REALCLI provides a rigorous, reproducible foundation for measuring and advancing collaborative CLI agents.

top_articles.title: AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
top_articles.title_original: AtomSD: Procedural Atom-Guided Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) possess broad factual knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, but solving complex tasks also requires procedural knowledge about how to act. Existing approaches often represent procedural knowledge through trajectories or bundled skills, limiting flexible reuse across interaction histories. This paper introduces Procedural Atoms, fine-grained and independently applicable units that represent Intent, When, Do, and Avoid guidance. Building on this representation, we propose AtomSD, an Atom-guided Self-Distillation framework in which the learner continually extracts Procedural Atoms from its own successful trajectories and distills them into the evolving policy through Atom-conditioned supervision and task-reward optimization. Comprehensive experiments show that AtomSD consistently outperforms strong reward-based and distillation methods, exceeding the state-of-the-art baseline by up to 9.31 points in average performance. Further analyses demonstrate that the proposed Procedural Atoms provide effective guidance, highlighting the value of atom-level procedural knowledge for policy learning.

top_articles.title: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.title_original: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k, ASE improves average Mean@8 across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks over GRPO by 4.87 and 1.87 percentage points, respectively, under the same rollout budget.

top_articles.title: Expert-Guided Rubrics as Dense Reward Signals for Reinforcement Learning in Non-Verifiable Domains
top_articles.title_original: Expert-Guided Rubrics as Dense Reward Signals for Reinforcement Learning in Non-Verifiable Domains
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they must interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information under domain-specific constraints. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can train such agents from the consequences of their actions, recent successes largely rely on verifiable tasks with automatically computed binary rewards. In non-verifiable retrieval tasks, assessing query quality requires scarce subject-matter expert (SME) judgment that is inherently graded rather than binary. With Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), sparse rewards yield no useful learning signal when all sampled outputs within a group receive the same outcome, causing optimization to stall. We introduce a method that converts a small, fixed investment of SME judgment into a dense reward and combines it with retrieval-based metrics to form a hybrid, GRPO-compatible training signal. Experiments show improvements of up to 6\% in Recall@3 and 6.7\% in MRR@3 compared with sparse-reward baselines.

top_articles.title: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
top_articles.title_original: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic studies of large language models localize function in parameters, attention heads or neurons, but those parts do not specify how one inference unfolds. We treat the ordered layer-state trajectory as the empirical process and test whether layer order defines a measurable computation. Across representative Qwen, Llama and Gemma checkpoints, realized order produced paths 1.60--2.24 times as aligned with their endpoint chord as endpoint-preserving shuffles. The order effect transferred to a lexical task, but was stronger in three random initializations of the same Qwen architecture, identifying an architecture-compatible scaffold rather than a training-specific law. Direct hidden states provided stronger mechanism coordinates than vocabulary readbacks, and a task-defined coordinate made candidate competition computable. After additive interventions failed, local transition actuators selectively controlled internal trajectories across checkpoints. A confidence gate then drove 17 of 87 held-out Qwen closure trajectories across the full-vocabulary top-1 candidate boundary while leaving all 203 non-closure top-1 outputs unchanged. Safety-matched action reassignment performed similarly, locating the gain in selective gating and the bounded actuator family rather than fine-grained dose assignment. Layer order exposes an observable, computable and behaviourally consequential process of transformer inference without establishing a complete theory of LLM dynamics or control of answer correctness.
